newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche Telekom has strong rivals at home.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche Telekom has strong rivals at home.

text.p: Just weeks ahead of the huge public offering of Deutsche Telekom AG, a powerful line-up of new competitors is emerging in what is expected to be a fierce tussle for a sizeable share of the former monopoly's home market.

Some of Germany's largest companies, together with big international telecoms groups, are combining know-how and networks and seem ready to spend in excess of $10 billion over the next 10 years to enter Europe's biggest telecoms market.

The contenders are hoping to carve up amongst themselves around a third of the German business, which is expected to be worth more than 100 billion marks ($65 billion) by the year 2000, once basic public telecommunication service is deregulated in 1998.

The latest turn of the carousel of ever-changing alliances came on Wednesday when RWE AG defected from its partnership with British Telecom and Viag AG to a tie-up with Veba AG and British-based Cable and Wireless.

The deal creates a powerful challenger that will turn up the pressure on Deutsche Telekom and that also has some of the key parts in place to offer a full range of services -- mobile communications, cable television and corporate networks.

Until now, the main threat to Telekom seemed to be coming from the DBKom alliance of Mannesmann AG, the German railway Deutsche Bahn AG and AT&T Corp, which is setting up a second national telecommunications network.
The departure of RWE from the alliance with BT and Viag, leaves the British phone giant suddenly on the search for a new partner that can offer some of the same network resources.
In Munich Thursday Viag chairman Georg Obermeier said BT and Viag would stand by their plans to integrate their telecommunications activities despite RWE's departure.
Thyssen, which lost to Mannesmann in its bid for DBKom, is further marginalised by the deal. Analysts said Thyssen could now be a potential partner for BT. Thyssen declined to comment.
The latest realignment underscores just how shaky many of the alliances are as companies seek the right blend of finances, physical resources and agreement on strategy.
"The new players have a very strong incentive to join forces," said Torsten Gerpott, telecommunications expert and professor at Duisburg University.
"But remember, RWE also bailed out of an alliance with Mannesmann before joining BT and Viag. You have to wonder whether it is a reliable partner now."
Some of the new competitors have already taken advantage of the gradual opening of the German telecommunications market.

Mannesmann operates the D2 digital cellular network with over two million connections. It has also built a nationwide backbone network based on asynchronous transfer mode (ATM) technology. ATM makes it possible to simultaneously transmit voice, data, fax and video over a single network.

Veba and Thyssen are big shareholders in E-Plus, Germany's third mobile phone network. Veba recently completed its own ATM network and operates corporate networks. It also has some 1.2 million cable TV subscribers.

But the sheer size of Deutsche Telekom and its direct access to more than 40 million customers means it will probably be decades before any of its competitors will be in the same position to offer comprehensive telecommunications services.
The newcomers are expected to first attack Telekom's most vulnerable flanks -- long-distance and international calls and internal networks for businesses.
But the greatest challenge is direct access to the customer in the "local loop", the stretch of communications cable from the nearest exchange to a customer's home or business.

DBKom hopes to get close to the customer by putting cable along the railway tracks. Veba and RWE will do the same alongside power lines and have local alliances with municipal utilities. But they still fall far short of the customer.

German lawmakers made an attempt to shift some of the balance in favour of the newcomers in the new telecoms law by stating that telecoms companies must grant access to their networks for competitors.
Called interconnection in industry jargon, this makes it possible for companies without networks to offer services over the networks of other firms, usually monopolies like Telekom.

But the German government is in a tough position. It must regulate competition, which means making sure that newcomers get a fair chance. But it must also make sure that state-owned Telekom's 15-billion-mark listing is a success.
"There is no question that they are not going to kill the goose that lays the golden egg," said Keith Mallinson, analyst with Yankee Group Europe.
Gerpott said the German government still had a long way to go before the regulatory environment shifted away from protecting Telekom in favour of promoting open competition.
"The telecoms law is so vague that it will take years before the regulatory environment is clear," he said.
"The Federal Communications Commission in the United States has written 700 pages of law on interconnection alone. Germany has just five pages, so there's a lot of work to be done."
This uncertainty about the law and the opportunities companies will have to compete is part of what has caused tensions in the relationships between alliance partners.
In the case of RWE, Viag and British Telecom, RWE was not as convinced as its partners that new, wireless technology could be used effectively to gain access to the local loop.

Instead of laying miles of cable, individual homes and businesses can be connected using wireless local loop technology to wireless communications networks. This cuts the costs of high interconnection fees for new operators.
A recent report by telecommunications analysts at Merrill Lynch states that such networks "can be constructed at up to one-fifth the cost of a fixed network".

Commenting on differences with RWE, a BT spokesman said: "Do you believe that mobile is the way the world is going, or do you believe it will stay fixed? BT and Viag believe in fixed/mobile integration and RWE didn't."
Although it is hard to say now who will be proven right, RWE chairman Dietmar Kuhnt warned against underestimating the challenge posed by Deutsche Telekom's sheer size.

"Only powerful alliances with a broad and comprehensive product offering will be able to survive," he said. "Our business policy was and is directed at being able to make a complete alternative offer to Deutsche Telekom from 1998."
Although the German government seems to be taking its time in prying open Telekom's local networks, there could be help on the way from the European Commission.
European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert is preparing a study on how cable television networks can be used to promote telecoms competition in local networks in Europe.
Telekom is in some ways a double monopoly. It owns both the public phone network and the cable TV network, which is the only alternative network that has access millions of homes.

Telekom's competitors would like the government to force it to sell the cable TV network. That is unlikely to happen. But it is widely expected that Brussels will put pressure on Bonn after Telekom's listing to open the network for competitors.
"Nothing will happen before early 1997," said Gerpott. "But next year, the EU will exert additional pressure on Deutsche Telekom to open the cable TV network to third-providers."
